subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
description: Students understand that a sample is examined to learn about a larger population, that conclusions drawn from a sample are valid only when the sample is representative, and that random sampling tends to produce representative samples that support valid inferences. They distinguish population from sample, identify biased versus unbiased sampling methods, recognize random sampling techniques, and judge whether a stated generalization about a population is justified by how the sample was collected.
subSkills: Distinguish the population (the whole group of interest) from a sample (the subset actually examined)
Define a representative sample as one whose characteristics mirror those of the population
Recognize that random sampling gives every member of the population an equal chance of selection
Identify common sampling methods (simple random, convenience, voluntary response, systematic) and classify them as random or non-random
Detect sources of bias (location bias, self-selection, leading questions, sampling only an unrepresentative subgroup)
Judge whether a generalization or inference about a population is valid given how the sample was chosen

problemArchetypes.name: Identify population vs. sample
problemArchetypes.example: A principal wants to know the favorite lunch of all $850$ students at a school. She surveys $50$ students. Identify the population and the sample.

problemArchetypes.name: Classify the sampling method
problemArchetypes.example: A reporter interviews the first $20$ people leaving a movie theater about the film. Is this a random sample or a convenience sample?

problemArchetypes.name: Detect bias in a sampling plan
problemArchetypes.example: To learn how all city residents commute, a researcher surveys only people waiting at a bus stop. Explain why this sample is biased.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the best (most representative) sampling method
problemArchetypes.example: A school of $600$ students wants opinions on a new dress code. Which plan gives the most representative sample: surveying the basketball team, surveying students whose ID numbers are drawn from a hat, or asking volunteers to email their opinions?

problemArchetypes.name: Judge the validity of an inference
problemArchetypes.example: From a random sample of $40$ of the $500$ books in a library, $10$ are mysteries. A student concludes about $\frac{1}{4}$ of all library books are mysteries. Is this inference valid? Why or why not?

Easy.description: Single-concept recall and identification from a clearly stated scenario. The student names the population or sample, or labels one sampling method as random or not random, with no competing considerations.
constraints: Scenario states the whole group and the surveyed subset explicitly
Only one concept is tested per item (population, sample, or random vs. non-random)
The correct answer follows directly from a single definition
No multi-part reasoning and no quantitative estimate required

Medium.description: Student must apply a definition to a less obvious scenario: identify the type of sampling, name the specific source of bias, or decide whether a sample is representative. Requires connecting the method used to its effect on representativeness.
constraints: Sampling method must be classified into a named category (convenience, voluntary response, simple random, systematic)
Bias must be identified AND its cause stated
Scenario contains a plausible but flawed plan that looks reasonable at first
May require comparing two plans to decide which is less biased

Hard.description: Multi-step reasoning that combines validity of inference with the quality of the sampling method, possibly including a simple proportional estimate from sample data, and an explanation of whether the resulting generalization is justified.
constraints: Student must evaluate whether a stated conclusion is valid given the sampling method
May require a proportional estimate from the sample (e.g. scale $\frac{10}{40}$ up to a population of $500$) and then judge whether that estimate is trustworthy
Requires distinguishing 'large sample' from 'representative sample' (size alone does not fix bias)
Answer must justify reasoning, not just state random or biased

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student swaps population and sample, treating the surveyed subset as the population
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels the $50$ surveyed students as the population and the $850$ students as the sample

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes any large sample is automatically representative, ignoring how it was selected
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Calls a biased convenience sample valid simply because many people were surveyed

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks a convenience or voluntary-response sample is random because it was not deliberately rigged
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Classifies surveying the first $20$ people leaving a theater as a random sample

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes a generalization is valid whenever the math (proportion) is computed correctly, regardless of bias
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts an inference about the whole population drawn from a self-selected subgroup because the percentage was calculated right

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the most convenient or easiest-to-reach group as the 'best' sample
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses surveying the basketball team over a drawn-from-a-hat random sample because they are easy to ask

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student equates representative with simply asking people who are available or interested
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a voluntary email response plan as representative because everyone had the chance to respond
